summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in identity documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker, available from 2022, remain valid until expiry. The policy is under challenge in the federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. Transgender and non-binary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked during processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage is not available in practice. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it, so the territory deliberately declined a formal ban before the 2015 federal ruling. In July 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory unsure whether that ruling applied: its attorney general said applicability was "still being reviewed... I don't know", while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the CNMI moved to apply it, and no licence applications had been made. In January 2016 the Senate-confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told his confirmation hearing that he had not read Obergefell, that the district court "doesn't deal with this ruling", and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws changed.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply despite officials' statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. No same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date, and the article sets out the litigation route: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the US Department of the Interior. On-island the local ban is still treated as operative and its constitutional durability as open: a July 2024 survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the ban would survive a 14th Amendment challenge, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act of 13 December 2022 obliged recognition of marriages performed elsewhere.

Transgender people have obtained protection in American Samoa through federal employment enforcement. In September 2023 the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 federal civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. Violence against transgender residents has also been prosecuted: in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.
tangentialFactors:
Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, is described in Pacific gender-identity scholarship as a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride with the phrase "we are fa'afafine Samoa"; the same scholarship frames a history of colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Social climate reporting is favourable but conservative in register. A 2009 expert column for Out Traveler stated that, unlike the homophobia then described as rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture, while noting that both Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system and that reserved behaviour by people of all orientations is expected. The same source reported Western gay men being courted by fa'afafine locals and by officially straight men, and quoted local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calling the Samoan islands "the homeland of fa'afafine culture". That account is sixteen years old and anecdotal rather than surveyed.

Comparison with the other United States territories is unflattering on marriage. Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply the 2015 federal marriage ruling, while American Samoa did not, and its judiciary was still operating in January 2016 on the premise that the ruling did not automatically reach the territory.
localsOnly:
Residents live under a chiefly fa'amatai system in which reserved conduct is expected of people of all orientations, so visible same-sex or gender-nonconforming expression attracts social restraint rather than legal sanction. Local gender-diverse residents have themselves contested the marriage question: at the 2003 committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine "don't believe in marriages with other men", describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing.

The territorial government is an established defendant in transgender employment litigation and has already settled with the United States Justice Department over the harassment of a transgender employee, so residents have a working federal enforcement route against their own administration. Resident passport and document holders are subject to the same federal binary-sex rules as visitors, with no territorial override reported in the sources.

The territory's marriage law is under active academic scrutiny on-island, including a 2024 survey by a Miami University professor examining both the constitutional durability of the local ban and the cultural orientation of the population, which indicates the question is being researched locally rather than settled.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling is operative in American Samoa is unresolved in the sources: a 2026 legal analysis says it applies and that a certificate must be issued, while territorial officials since 2015 have said otherwise and the local statutory ban is still treated on-island as operative. No same-sex marriage licence application has been recorded, so the conflict has never been tested in the High Court of American Samoa.

The text and current amendment status of the territory's own marriage statute are not sourced here; the 2003 bill was defeated, but whether an earlier or later ban exists in the code is not stated.

Whether the EO 14201 visa restriction and its SWS25 marking apply to persons entering American Samoa specifically, as opposed to the mainland, is not sourced. Nor is territory-specific procedure for name or sex-marker changes on local records; the available guidance is general legal-organisation advice on federal documents.

The practical availability of gender-affirming care in American Samoa, and whether the care-funding orders affect any locally delivered service, are not sourced. The 2009 social-climate account is dated and journalistic rather than surveyed.
